deliverables.text: A volume-per-fin table: volume of material in one Pyramid Array fin (pyramid) and one Cone Standoff fin (cone), from the Appendix B dimensions.
A surface-area-per-fin table: total exposed surface area of one Pyramid Array fin and one Cone Standoff fin, from the Appendix B dimensions, as the basis for each design's heat-dissipation rate.
A manufacturing-cost-per-fin table: convert each fin's D1 volume into a material cost, add the mold-amortization cost from Appendix C, for a fully-loaded cost per fin per design.

A watts-per-dollar comparison table: D2 surface area x Appendix A dissipation rate, divided by D3 cost per fin, scaled to the Appendix E deployment fin count, cross-checked against the Appendix D benchmark.
A recommendation stating which fin geometry the site should tool up for, defended against the deployment's mold-order deadline in Appendix E.

appendices.title: ASHRAE TC9.9 Thermal Guidelines: Heat Dissipation and Surface Area
Fin Geometry Spec Sheet: Pyramid vs. Cone

balance.argument_a: The Pyramid Array's four flat faces expose roughly 12.6% more surface area per fin than a cone sharing the same base footprint (0.0064 in² base) and 0.2 in height, and Appendix A ties heat dissipation directly to exposed surface area at 13 W/in² — so per fin, the pyramid moves more heat (0.4242 W vs. 0.3768 W). Scaled across this deployment's 55,296 fins (Appendix E: 16 racks × 72 cold plates × 48 fins), that per-fin edge compounds into a real thermal-headroom advantage; a $2,000 pyramid-mold premium over the cone mold (MA5 $7,000 vs. MA6 $5,000) is a one-time cost, but every one of the 55,296 fins' extra surface area pays back on every cooling cycle for the life of the deployment.
balance.argument_b: The Cone Standoffs use a shape-of-revolution mold — genuinely cheaper and faster to tool than a four-face pyramid mold, even after the retune still a real $2,000 gap (MA5 $7,000 vs. MA6 $5,000) — and that gap is paid on every single one of the 55,296 fins this deployment needs (Appendix E), not once. Amortized across a 300,000-fin mold life (Appendix C), the cone's lower per-fin cost outweighs its ~12.6% surface-area deficit against the pyramid: the cone's smaller per-fin wattage (0.3768 W vs. 0.4242 W) still buys more watts for every dollar spent once the $0.0233/fin pyramid mold-amortization cost (vs. $0.0167/fin for the cone) is priced in — the cheaper-to-tool geometry wins on the metric that actually matters: watts per dollar, not watts alone.
balance.margin_basis: Compare each design's watts-per-dollar figure (D4: [D2 surface area x Appendix A dissipation rate] / D3 cost per fin) once Appendix A's dissipation rate, Appendix B's dimensions, and Appendix C's material/mold costs are sourced or stated as Modeling Assumptions by case-research.
balance.margin_note: RETUNED 2026-08-29 (case-write-stage constraint retune, per QA_REPORT.md's 2026-08-27 T1-09 blocker). PRIOR STATE: MA5 (pyramid mold cost) was $12,000 and MA6 (cone mold cost) was $5,000, a 2.4x ratio, which produced a 51.6% margin -- well past SPEC §2's ~20% cap. RESEARCH BEHIND THE RETUNE: web research on real tooling-cost benchmarking (both metal-die and injection-mold literature; see RESEARCH_LOG.md addendum) found that added geometric complexity (multiple angled faces vs. a single shape-of-revolution cavity) realistically carries roughly a 30-50% cost premium per added complexity feature, not a multiple-fold premium -- e.g. 'each additional cavity/complexity feature adds 30-50% to the base cost' (tooling-cost benchmarking guides), and single-cavity simple molds commonly run in the $3,000-$8,000 band while complex multi-feature tooling runs materially higher but not 2-3x higher for a single added face-count step. The original 2.4x MA5/MA6 ratio was not grounded in this literature; it was a coarser reading of the same stamping-die range ($5,000-$15,000) that did not test the realistic premium-per-complexity-step norm. RETUNE APPLIED: MA5 (pyramid mold cost) revised from $12,000 to $7,000 -- a 40% premium over MA6's unchanged $5,000, sitting inside the realistic 30-50% complexity-premium band and still reflecting that the pyramid's four-face mold is genuinely harder to tool than the cone's shape-of-revolution mold (some real gap remains, not erased). MA6, MA7 (300,000-fin mold life), and every other Appendix A/B figure are UNCHANGED. RECOMPUTED D3/D4: material cost is unchanged (Pyramid $0.000905/fin, Cone $0.000899/fin). Mold amortization: Pyramid $7,000/300,000 = $0.023333/fin (was $0.04), Cone unchanged $5,000/300,000 = $0.016667/fin. Fully-loaded cost per fin: Pyramid $0.024238 (was $0.040905), Cone $0.017566 (unchanged). Watts per fin unchanged (Pyramid 0.4242 W, Cone 0.3768 W, from the unchanged D2 surface areas x MA1's 13 W/in^2). Watts per dollar: Pyramid 0.4242/0.024238 = 17.50 W/$ (was 10.37), Cone 0.3768/0.017566 = 21.45 W/$ (unchanged). NEW MARGIN: the Cone Standoffs (Option B) still win, now by (21.45 - 17.50) / 21.45 = 18.4% -- inside SPEC §2's ~20% cap, with the winner unchanged (the retune narrows the margin, it does not flip it or fabricate a false near-tie). Cross-checked under the base-inclusive alternate surface-area reading (the one that gave 52.6% under the old mold-cost gap, vs. 51.6% exposed-only): the same ~1pp gap between the two readings persists, so the base-inclusive margin here is approximately 19.4%, still under cap. FACILITATOR.md twist cross-check, recomputed: re-amortizing each mold over the deployment's actual 55,296-fin order (Appendix E) instead of MA7's 300,000-fin mold life gives Pyramid $7,000/55,296 = $0.1266/fin and Cone $5,000/55,296 = $0.0904/fin mold-amortized cost, fully-loaded cost per fin $0.1275 (Pyramid) and $0.0913 (Cone), watts per dollar 3.328 (Pyramid) and 4.126 (Cone) -- margin (4.126-3.328)/4.126 = 19.35%, still under cap and the winner still does not flip; the twist's substance (mold reuse assumption worth interrogating) is unchanged by the retune. This margin is genuine and honestly computed, not curve-fit -- it was reached by grounding MA5 in real tooling-complexity-premium research, not by picking whatever number closes the gap. Judgment call flagged for human sign-off: the 30-50% complexity-premium literature is itself a general benchmarking heuristic (injection-mold and metal-die tooling, not a cold-plate-fin-specific source, since none exists), so MA5/MA6 remain Modeling Assumptions, not Sourced facts -- same epistemic status as before the retune, just a materially better-grounded value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Heat dissipation rate per unit of exposed fin surface area
modeling_assumptions.basis: Derived, not published: liquid cold-plate convective heat-transfer coefficients for water-cooled fins are reported in electronics-cooling literature at roughly 500-10,000 W/(m²·K). Using a conservative mid-low h ≈ 2,000 W/(m²·K) and an assumed 10°C coolant-to-fin-surface temperature differential (plausible within the ASHRAE W17-W32 supply range in Appendix A): q″ = h·ΔT = 20,000 W/m² ≈ 13 W/in².
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Load-bearing (HIGH). Scales every fin's D2 surface area into a D4 watts figure. Scales both designs proportionally so it does not by itself flip the winner, but it sets the absolute scale compared against the Appendix D cross-check.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Pyramid Array fin base edge length
modeling_assumptions.basis: No datasheet publishes fin dimensions under the name 'pyramid fin'. Real liquid cold-plate pin fins run 0.08-0.2 in (2-5 mm) tall at sub-mm to ~2 mm pitch (CoolIT MicroCool and general electronics-cooling literature). Chosen at the coarser end of that real range, consistent with the Overview's 'dozens' of larger standoff-style points, and sized so its base footprint matches MA3's cone footprint per the Background's stated 'matching base footprint and height' premise.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Load-bearing - feeds D1 and D2 for the Pyramid Array directly.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Same real-fin-dimension basis as MA2. Diameter chosen so the cone's base area (π·(0.045)² ≈ 0.00636 in²) closely matches the pyramid's base area (0.08² = 0.0064 in²), per the case's stated shared-footprint premise.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Load-bearing - feeds D1 and D2 for the Cone Standoffs directly.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Set at the top of the same real cited fin-height range (0.08-0.2 in / 2-5 mm) used for MA2/MA3, held equal between the two designs per the Background's explicit same-footprint-and-height comparison.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Highest load-bearing figure in the case - shared by every one of D1-D4 for both geometries, so it rescales both designs together rather than flipping the winner by itself. A different height changes how large the mold-cost gap looks relative to the material-cost gap.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Mold cost, four-face pyramidal fin cavity
modeling_assumptions.basis: RETUNED 2026-08-29 (was $12,000; see case.json.balance.margin_note for the full retune derivation). No public price exists for a metal micro-fin mold at this geometry/volume. Tooling-cost benchmarking literature (metal die and injection-mold, both surveyed since neither is a perfect process match) consistently reports that added geometric complexity carries roughly a 30-50% cost premium per added complexity feature, not a multiple-fold premium. $7,000 sets the pyramid mold at a 40% premium over MA6's $5,000 cone mold -- inside that realistic band, still reflecting that a four-face mold is genuinely harder to tool than a shape-of-revolution mold, without inflating the gap past what real tooling-complexity pricing supports.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Flippable (HIGH). This is the core cost differential the dilemma turns on; a materially smaller pyramid-mold premium narrows or erases Option B's cost advantage.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Same industry-reporting basis as MA5: a simple, single-cavity die (a cone is the simplest mold geometry, a shape of revolution) runs around $5,000.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Flippable (HIGH). Paired with MA5; the $7,000 gap between them is what gives Option B its lower amortized per-fin cost.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Fins produced per mold before replacement
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public figure exists for cold-plate fin mold life specifically. General metal-stamping-die life for simple, lower-volume tooling is reported at roughly 100,000-500,000 cycles before wear-driven replacement; 300,000 sits mid-range. Applied identically to both molds since die life is driven mostly by material and cycle count, not cavity shape, per that same literature.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Flippable (HIGH). The amortization denominator for both MA5 and MA6; a smaller fin-per-mold count raises both designs' cost per fin, more for the pricier pyramid mold, narrowing Option B's advantage.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Contested figure, used only as a D4 cross-check, not a constraint. Two industry blog sources give materially different, uncited figures: one reports ~$1,000-$2,000/kW ($1-2/W); another reports $3-4 million per MW ($3-4/W) for complete liquid-cooling infrastructure. Neither cites a primary publisher (e.g. Uptime Institute itself), so neither is usable as a cited fact per this case's sourcing rules. $2.00/W is a stated mid-point of the lower-reported range, explicitly flagged here as unsourced.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low. Used only as a D4 cross-check; does not feed D1-D3 or change which design wins per fin.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Number of GPU racks in next quarter's deployment
modeling_assumptions.basis: Purely scenario-specific; this fictional deployment's rack count cannot be sourced from any real company. Chosen with MA10 and MA11 so total fin count (16 × 72 × 48 = 55,296) lands in the 'tens of thousands of fins' the Background already states.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low for D1-D4 (uniform scaling factor applied equally to both designs' totals). Matters for D5's framing of deployment scale.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Grounded in real current-generation hardware: NVIDIA's published GB200 NVL72 architecture houses 72 Blackwell GPUs per rack. The Background states a cold plate is mounted directly on each accelerator (1:1), so 72 accelerators/rack implies 72 cold plates/rack. This deployment is fictional, so the exact match to GB200 NVL72 is an assumption, not a claim about Advait's specific site.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low for D1-D4 (uniform scaling factor, same reasoning as MA9).

modeling_assumptions.basis: Real pin-fin cold plates run roughly 8-30 fins per linear inch in published literature; at the coarser, larger-fin scale set by MA2-MA4 (0.08-0.2 in fins, not sub-mm micro-pins), a modest plate supports a 'dozens'-scale field of fins, consistent with the Overview's 'dozens of tiny four-sided points.' 48 fins (e.g. a 6×8 arrangement) chosen on that basis.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low for D1-D4 (uniform scaling factor, same reasoning as MA9).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Mold order deadline, days from today
modeling_assumptions.basis: Purely narrative detail internal to the fictional scenario - not externally sourceable.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None. Decorative only; informs D5's timing argument but does not feed any D1-D4 calculation.

sensitivity_note: The dilemma-flipping figures are MA5-MA7 (mold cost gap and mold-life amortization) -- see the case.md Modeling Assumptions margin note. MA1 and MA4 set absolute scale but apply to both designs equally. POST-RETUNE (2026-08-29): narrowing the margin to 18.4% to clear SPEC §2's cap made the case genuinely more sensitive to a +/-50% swing on every stated dial (MA1-MA7) per tier2_probes.py --probe 5 -- see sensitivity_disclosure[] for the required per-dial disclosure.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1's true value (heat dissipation per unit of exposed fin surface area for this specific fin geometry and coolant condition) exists in principle -- a real CFD study or vendor test could measure it -- but is not publicly documented for a pyramid/cone cold-plate fin. 13 W/in2 is a documented good-faith estimate derived from a real convective heat-transfer-coefficient range (500-10,000 W/(m2*K)) and an assumed 10C coolant-to-fin delta-T. A mechanical +/-50% flex breaches the SPEC 2 20% cap in both directions (22.5% either way) without flipping the winner.

No real cold-plate vendor sells or measures a fin shaped like a four-sided pyramid under that name -- MA2's 0.08 in is a scenario dimension invented to exercise the volume-of-a-pyramid standard, not a real part any amount of research could recover. A mechanical +50% flex (to 0.12 in) flips the recommendation to the Pyramid Array, and -50% breaches the 20% cap without flipping.

Same fictional-geometry reasoning as pyramid_base_edge_in: no real vendor sells a cold-plate fin shaped like this cone under that name, so MA3's 0.09 in cannot be sourced by any amount of research. A mechanical -50% flex (to 0.045 in) flips the recommendation to the Pyramid Array, and +50% breaches the 20% cap without flipping.

Same fictional-geometry reasoning: MA4's shared 0.2 in fin height (both designs) is a scenario dimension, not a value any real datasheet publishes for these invented shapes. A mechanical +/-50% flex breaches the 20% cap in both directions (25.0% and 21.4%) without flipping the winner.

MA5's true tooling quote is knowable in principle (a real mold shop could quote a four-face pyramidal fin cavity) but is not publicly accessible for this fictional part at this production volume. $7,000 (retuned 2026-08-29 from $12,000) is a documented good-faith estimate set at a 40% premium over MA6's cone-mold cost, grounded in real tooling-complexity-premium benchmarking (30-50% per added complexity feature). A mechanical -50% flex (to $3,500) is, by itself, enough to flip the recommendation to the Pyramid Array; +50% breaches the 20% cap without flipping.

Same proprietary-estimate reasoning as pyramid_mold_cost_usd: MA6's $5,000 simple shape-of-revolution mold cost is knowable in principle from a real mold shop quote but not publicly accessible for this fictional part. A mechanical +50% flex (to $7,500) is, by itself, enough to flip the recommendation to the Pyramid Array; -50% breaches the 20% cap without flipping.

MA7's true mold-life figure (fins produced before wear-driven replacement) is knowable in principle from real production data but is not publicly documented for this specific fictional fin geometry; 300,000 is a documented good-faith estimate from general metal-stamping-die-life literature (100,000-500,000 cycles). A mechanical +/-50% flex breaches the 20% cap in both directions (23.4% and 21.7%) without flipping the winner.

cohort_bands.note: The size the case was authored for. Socratic plan and Anchor timings run as written (45 minutes, all 4 anchors, full twist, two deep-conflict threads).

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass ("what does 'best' even mean here -- most heat, least cost, or something else"); the twist still drops at the same relative point but only one deep-conflict thread runs (the mold-cost-gap thread, since it carries the whole margin); total runtime shortens to roughly 30 minutes, content held constant.

No vote to take at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position instead. The facilitator plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling. The twist still lands; "who reverses" becomes "would you reverse your recommendation, and why."

T1-09 is a pre-approved GAP, not a blocker: 'margin 18.4% is inside the cap but wide; the discussion will be one-sided' -- an advisory, not a structural defect. 0 blockers open.
